- Generator scaffolding left in: oaicite, [cite: 1], placeholders -- finish the text and read it
- The "it's not X, it's Y" construction -- just state Y
- A bolded word opening a list item as a per-item tag -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- Saying "is" the long way: serves as, boasts, functions as -- use the plain verb
- One-line dramatic fragments: "That's it. That's the whole thing." -- cut them, the preceding sentence already made the point
- Em dashes clustering in one document -- most drafts need 0-2; use commas, periods or parentheses for the rest
- Filler verbs: leverages, facilitates, unlocks -- use a plain verb, or cut the sentence
- A snake_case identifier written as plain prose -- name it in words, or mark it as inline code
- Marketing cliches: "hidden gem", "let's dive in" -- say the specific thing
- The "Not X. Not Y." listing construction -- state the point once
- Stock section skeleton: "Despite its success", "Looking ahead" -- name the specific thing the section is for
- Standalone filler adverbs: undoubtedly, arguably, notably, importantly, ultimately -- most add nothing; cut them unless one is carrying real emphasis
- A banned synonym of one of this project's canonical terms, per its declared lexicon -- one word, one meaning: use the canonical term the word's own note names
- Dramatic turning points with nothing concrete behind them: "Everything changed." -- name the actual event, or cut it

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a short announcement for a new feature in a note-taking app: offline sync. Around 200 words.

Your notes now sync offline.

Write on a plane, in a tunnel, anywhere the connection drops, and your changes save locally the moment you make them. When the network comes back, everything merges in the background. No spinner, no "reconnecting" banner, no lost paragraph.

If you edit the same note on two devices while both are offline, we keep both versions and let you pick what to keep, instead of silently overwriting one. Conflicts show up as a simple side-by-side comparison, not a merge conflict dump.

This also fixes the flaky-wifi problem: spotty coffee-shop connections used to cause failed saves and duplicate notes. Now the app queues changes and sends them when the connection is stable, so a bad signal costs you nothing.

Offline sync works across iOS, Android, and desktop, and rolls out to all users this week. No settings to change and no toggle to find. It just works the way you'd expect a notebook to work: open it anywhere, write, and trust it's there next time you open the app.

Your notes now sync with local-first sync.

Write on a plane, in a tunnel, anywhere the connection drops, and your changes save locally the moment you make them. When the network comes back, everything merges in the background. No spinner, no "reconnecting" banner, no lost paragraph.

If you edit the same note on two devices while both are offline, the app keeps both versions instead of overwriting one with the other. When the devices reconnect, you get a side-by-side comparison of the two versions and pick which parts to keep, or keep both as separate notes.

This also fixes the flaky-wifi problem: spotty coffee-shop connections used to cause failed saves and duplicate notes. Now the app queues changes and sends them when the connection is stable, so a bad signal costs you nothing.

Local-first sync works across iOS, Android, and desktop, and rolls out to all users this week. No settings to change and no toggle to find. It works the way you'd expect a notebook to work: open it anywhere, write, and trust it's there next time you open the app.
